baicapil.summary: A branded baicalin-themed cosmetic active in scalp serums, used by people with thinning hair hoping for less shedding and a fuller look.

quick.overview:
Baicapil is a branded cosmetic ingredient in scalp serums made for thinning hair. Its name points to baicalin, a plant flavonoid from skullcap. People use it hoping for less shedding and hair that looks denser.

The idea is a calmer scalp that supports the follicles, so fewer hairs fall out. A 2025 review of cosmetic hair actives lists it, and no trial of the product itself was found.
quick.how: It is used as a leave-on scalp serum, applied as part of a regular routine and often alongside other thinning-hair products. Users generally judge it over several months of consistent use.
quick.risks: No safety data specific to the product were found. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient, so it is not regulated as a drug. As with any scalp product, irritation is possible.

angle.text: Baicapil is a branded scalp-serum active people use for thinning hair. The idea is that a baicalin-based ingredient calms the scalp and supports follicles, so you shed less and hair looks fuller. No trial of the product itself was found.

dihydroquercetin-glucoside.summary: A taxifolin derivative that is one half of the Redensyl serum active, used by people with thinning hair hoping for thicker-looking scalp hair.

quick.overview:
Dihydroquercetin glucoside (DHQG) is a sugar-linked form of taxifolin, a plant flavonoid, and is one of the two components of the Redensyl hair-growth active. People use Redensyl serums hoping for thicker-looking scalp hair.

The marketing claim is that it stimulates follicle stem cells. No study of DHQG alone was found; small studies have tested finished serums, and a 2025 review discusses Redensyl among topical hair actives.
quick.how: It is used as a leave-on scalp serum, usually as part of a daily or regular routine and often alongside other thinning-hair products. Users typically judge results over several months.
quick.risks: Taxifolin is reported as non-mutagenic in bacterial tests. No human safety data for DHQG itself were found. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient.

angle.text: DHQG is one of the two components of Redensyl, a cosmetic active in serums for thinning hair. The claim is that it stimulates follicle stem cells for thicker-looking hair. The supporting data come from Redensyl-containing serums rather than the component alone.

egcg-glucoside.summary: A green-tea catechin derivative that is the partner component in Redensyl serums, used for thicker-looking scalp hair.

quick.overview:
EGCG-glucoside is a sugar-linked version of EGCG, the main catechin in green tea. It is named as one of the two components of Redensyl, a cosmetic active used on thinning scalp hair, alongside DHQG.

The appeal is thicker-looking hair through increased follicle activity. The only study found on the glucoside itself looked at a digestive enzyme in a lab dish, not hair; EGCG has wider research in other areas.
quick.how: It is used as part of Redensyl-type leave-on scalp serums, applied regularly over months and often alongside other thinning-hair products.
quick.risks: High oral intakes of EGCG are linked to liver toxicity according to EFSA. No safety data for the topical glucoside were found.

angle.text: EGCG-glucoside is the green-tea-derived partner of DHQG in Redensyl, a cosmetic active for thinning hair. People use it hoping for more follicle activity and thicker-looking hair. Hair data on this component alone are lacking.

biochanin-a.summary: A red-clover isoflavone named in Capixyl scalp serums, used by people with thinning hair hoping for a fuller look.

quick.overview:
Biochanin A is a phytoestrogen from red clover and other legumes, named as a component of Capixyl, a cosmetic peptide-and-isoflavone active for thinning scalp hair. People use it hoping for less thinning and fuller-looking hair.

The proposed route is scalp-level hormone-pathway effects. In lab assays it binds estrogen receptors and weakly inhibits an enzyme; trials of red clover isoflavones have addressed menopause and bone, and no hair study of the compound was found.
quick.how: It is used as a leave-on scalp serum or lotion as part of a regular routine, often alongside other thinning-hair products, with results judged over months.
quick.risks: As a phytoestrogen it has hormone-receptor activity in lab work. No safety data for topical hair use were found.

angle.text: Biochanin A is a red-clover phytoestrogen named in Capixyl, a cosmetic active for thinning hair. The idea is that it acts on scalp hormone pathways to slow thinning and keep hair looking fuller. It has been studied for menopause and bone, and hair studies were not found.

suvomipic.summary: Pelage's experimental once-daily scalp gel for hair loss, in phase 2 with company-reported density gains.

quick.overview:
Suvomipic (PP405) is an experimental scalp gel from Pelage Pharmaceuticals aimed at androgenetic hair loss. People following hair loss research watch it as a possible new regrowth option.

It inhibits the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier, which is thought to push dormant follicle stem cells toward glycolysis and growth. In preliminary phase 2a results released in June 2025, 31% of men reached a hair density gain of 20% or more at eight weeks, with no placebo responders; the trial was designed mainly to assess safety.
quick.how: It is a once-daily topical used in clinical trials only. It is not available outside studies, and phase 3 trials were planned for 2026.
quick.risks: It is investigational and not approved anywhere. Safety data are early-phase and the results come from the company.

angle.text: Suvomipic is an experimental once-daily scalp gel that blocks the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier, which is thought to switch follicle stem cells toward growth and regrow scalp hair. Company-reported phase 2a results showed density gains at eight weeks.

quercitrin.summary: A plant flavonoid with antioxidant lab data, discussed for healthier-looking hair, with no human hair studies.

quick.overview:
Quercitrin is a flavonoid found in buckwheat, oak and some herbal extracts. It comes up in hair-health discussions for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity, with people hoping for healthier-looking hair.

The proposed chain is less oxidative stress at the follicle. In animal and cell studies it is broken down to quercetin and dampens inflammatory signalling such as NF-kappaB and iNOS; no human hair study was found.
quick.how: It is mostly encountered through plant foods and herbal extracts, and sometimes in supplements or topical blends aimed at hair, used as an add-on to a regular routine.
quick.risks: Dietary exposure through plant foods is common. Concentrated topical or supplement use has no published hair-related safety data.

angle.text: Quercitrin is a plant flavonoid people discuss for hair because of its antioxidant activity, the idea being less oxidative stress at the follicle and healthier-looking hair. Antioxidant data come from cell and animal work.

horsetail-extract.summary: A silica-rich herbal extract in hair and nail supplements and shampoos, used for stronger, thicker-looking hair.

quick.overview:
Horsetail extract comes from a fern-like plant and is sold in hair and nail supplements and shampoos as a silica source. Users hope for stronger hair shafts and nails and hair that looks thicker and less brittle.

The usual proposal is silica supporting the hair shaft. Lab studies show anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activity in cells, and at least two registered trials have tested multi-ingredient hair supplements; no single-ingredient hair trial was found.
quick.how: It is taken as a capsule or tea, or used in shampoos and tonics, usually as part of a hair-and-nail routine continued for several months.
quick.risks: The plant is toxic to livestock and may form nicotine in polluted conditions. Human safety data for hair-focused use are limited.

angle.text: Horsetail extract is sold in hair and nail supplements and shampoos as a silica source, with users hoping for a stronger hair shaft and thicker, less brittle hair. Lab data exist, and single-ingredient hair trials were not found.

isoflavones.summary: Soy-derived phytoestrogens discussed for slower thinning and fuller-looking hair, studied in people for other conditions.

quick.overview:
Isoflavones are estrogen-like compounds from soy and other legumes, mainly genistein and daidzein. People discuss them as a food or supplement route to slower thinning and fuller-looking hair.

They bind estrogen receptors weakly and are processed by gut bacteria, partly into equol, which is the basis for the idea of shifting hair-cycle signalling. Human research covers cancer, bone, menopause and skin; no hair-specific study was found.
quick.how: People get them through soy foods or supplements, and sometimes topical products, as a long-term dietary habit rather than a quick fix.
quick.risks: Long-term supplement safety data are described as insufficient. EFSA found no adverse effects in postmenopausal women up to 150 mg per day, with data gaps noted.

angle.text: Soy isoflavones such as genistein and daidzein act as weak estrogens, and some users hope that shifts hair-cycle signalling toward slower thinning and fuller-looking hair. People have studied them for menopause, bone and skin rather than hair.

estrogen-topical-for-hair.summary: Scalp estrogen solutions, mainly alfatradiol, used to slow pattern hair loss, with reported slowing or stabilizing of loss.

quick.overview:
Topical estrogen for hair usually means alfatradiol (17-alpha-estradiol), a weak estrogen scalp solution sold in Germany and parts of Latin America for pattern hair loss. People use it to slow thinning and keep what they have.

It binds estrogen receptors weakly and inhibits 5-alpha-reductase, reducing conversion of testosterone to DHT and so follicle shrinkage. Studies report it slowing or stabilizing loss without increasing density or thickness, and minoxidil outperformed it in a 103-woman study.
quick.how: It is an alcohol-based solution applied to the scalp as a long-term routine, sometimes alongside other thinning-hair treatments.
quick.risks: Scalp irritation from the alcohol vehicle and more oil production are reported. Labeling advises against use in pregnancy and under age 18.

angle.text: Scalp estrogen solutions, mainly alfatradiol, weakly block 5-alpha-reductase so less DHT reaches the follicle, which slows shrinkage and thinning. Studies describe slowed or stabilized loss rather than added density.

triamcinolone-injections.summary: A clinician-administered steroid injection for patchy alopecia areata, with regrowth reported in most treated patients.

quick.overview:
Triamcinolone is a corticosteroid that dermatologists inject into patches of alopecia areata, an autoimmune cause of hair loss, to regrow hair in the patch. It is not used for ordinary pattern hair loss.

It is about five times as potent as cortisol and calms the local immune attack on follicles. A 2020 systematic review reported more than half regrowth in about 81 percent of treated patients, though hair often regrows on its own in patchy disease.
quick.how: It is given in a dermatologist's office as repeated injections into the bald patches, with regrowth judged over the following weeks to months.
quick.risks: It is prescription-only. Skin thinning is commonly described with skin injections, and injection near the eye has caused raised eye pressure and cases of endophthalmitis.

angle.text: Dermatologists inject triamcinolone into patches of alopecia areata to calm the immune attack on follicles so hair regrows in the patch. A 2020 review reported more than half regrowth in about 81 percent of treated patients.

deuruxolitinib.summary: Newly approved oral JAK inhibitor for severe alopecia areata, with strong regrowth in trials and a boxed warning.

quick.overview:
Deuruxolitinib (Leqselvi) is an oral prescription pill approved in the US for adults with severe alopecia areata, an autoimmune cause of scalp and body hair loss. People with extensive loss follow it for full regrowth.

It blocks JAK enzymes that relay inflammatory signals, which is thought to stop the immune attack on follicles. In the Phase 3 THRIVE-AA1 trial, adults with at least half of their scalp hair lost regrew significantly more hair than on placebo. It is not approved for pattern baldness.
quick.how: It is a daily pill prescribed and monitored by a doctor, with regrowth building over several months.
quick.risks: The label carries a boxed warning for serious infections, death, cancer, major cardiovascular events and blood clots. Common effects include headache, acne and raised cholesterol. It is contraindicated with certain CYP2C9 conditions and may harm a fetus.

angle.text: Deuruxolitinib is an oral JAK inhibitor approved in the US for severe alopecia areata. By easing the immune attack on follicles it lets scalp and body hair regrow, and trial participants regrew significantly more hair than on placebo.

ruxolitinib-oral.summary: Oral JAK inhibitor approved for blood and transplant disorders and followed off-label as an alopecia areata regrowth route.

quick.overview:
Oral ruxolitinib (Jakafi) is a prescription JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor approved for myelofibrosis, polycythemia vera and graft-versus-host disease. People with alopecia areata follow it as an off-label route to hair regrowth.

By blocking cytokine signalling in immune cells it is thought to ease the immune attack on follicles. Alopecia areata is listed as an area of investigation; other JAK inhibitors have approvals or trial data in that condition.
quick.how: It is a daily pill prescribed and monitored by a physician for its approved conditions; use for hair is off-label.
quick.risks: Reported effects include low blood counts, infections including shingles, and raised cholesterol and liver enzymes. Reviews discuss cancer and infection concerns for the JAK inhibitor class. Prescription only.

angle.text: Oral ruxolitinib blocks JAK1 and JAK2 signalling, which is thought to ease the immune attack on follicles in alopecia areata and allow regrowth. It is approved for blood and transplant conditions, and hair use is off-label.

methotrexate-for-alopecia.summary: Long-used immunosuppressant tried off-label for alopecia areata regrowth, backed by small studies and a 2019 meta-analysis.

quick.overview:
Methotrexate is an immunosuppressant prescribed off-label for alopecia areata, alone or with corticosteroids, to regrow patchy hair lost to autoimmune attack.

By suppressing immune activity it lessens the attack on follicles. A 2019 meta-analysis described definitive evidence as scarce; most data come from small studies, case series and retrospective cohorts, and newer JAK inhibitors are now compared against it in trials.
quick.how: It is a prescription drug taken under medical supervision with regular monitoring, and regrowth is judged over months.
quick.risks: It is a systemic immunosuppressant needing medical monitoring. A report described raised liver enzymes after scalp delivery sessions.

angle.text: Methotrexate suppresses immune activity, so follicles face less autoimmune attack and patchy hair can regrow in alopecia areata. It is used off-label, alone or with corticosteroids, and a 2019 meta-analysis found data mostly from small studies.

mometasone.summary: A potent steroid for allergies, asthma and eczema that comes up for scalp inflammation, with no hair-loss studies found.

quick.overview:
Mometasone furoate is a corticosteroid used in nasal sprays, inhalers and skin creams for allergy, asthma and eczema. It comes up in hair discussions for calming scalp inflammation, and because topical steroids as a class are associated with alopecia areata care.

It binds glucocorticoid receptors and dampens inflammatory signalling, giving calmer scalp skin. No study of mometasone for hair loss was found.
quick.how: The topical form is applied to inflamed skin, typically for short courses under a doctor's direction.
quick.risks: Listed risks include local infections, adrenal suppression with heavy exposure, skin thinning with prolonged topical use and fetal risk in animal studies.

angle.text: Mometasone is a potent steroid that dampens inflammation, so it comes up for calming an irritated scalp and as a relative of steroids used in alopecia areata. Hair-loss studies of mometasone itself were not found.

diaminopyrimidine-oxide.summary: A minoxidil-related cosmetic ingredient in hair lotions and shampoos, used for thicker-looking hair.

quick.overview:
Diaminopyrimidine oxide is a minoxidil-related ingredient in some hair-growth and anti-hair-loss lotions and shampoos. People with thinning hair use it hoping for thicker-looking hair.

Patents, including Korean filings from 2007 and 2008, describe such compositions as enhancing hair root activity. A 2026 network meta-analysis of therapies beyond minoxidil was reviewed, and no randomized trial of this ingredient was found.
quick.how: It is used in leave-on lotions or shampoos as part of a regular thinning-hair routine, with results judged over months.
quick.risks: No safety data were found in the reviewed sources. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient.

angle.text: Diaminopyrimidine oxide is a minoxidil-related ingredient in hair lotions and shampoos for thinning hair. Patents describe it as boosting hair root activity for thicker-looking hair. It is known mainly from patents, and trials were not found.

sarcosine-hair.summary: A glycine-derived amino acid listed in some hair-growth blends, used hoping to support follicle cells for fuller-looking hair.

quick.overview:
Sarcosine is a small naturally occurring amino acid, an N-methyl form of glycine. It is listed as a component in some hair-growth blends, with the idea that it supports follicle energy and cells for fuller-looking hair.

In the body it is an intermediate in choline-to-glycine metabolism. No clinical study of sarcosine for hair growth was found.
quick.how: It is encountered as one listed ingredient in topical or supplement blends used as part of a regular hair routine.
quick.risks: No hair-specific safety data were described in the sources reviewed. Its sarcosinate derivatives are widely used as surfactants in consumer products.

angle.text: Sarcosine is a glycine-derived amino acid listed in some hair-growth blends, with the idea that it supports follicle cells and energy for fuller-looking hair. Hair studies behind it were not found.

cinnamomum-zeylanicum-bark-extract.summary: Ceylon cinnamon bark extract listed in the Sepicontrol A5 cosmetic blend, used for scalp and hair support.

quick.overview:
This is an extract of the inner bark of the Ceylon cinnamon tree, described as one component of the Sepicontrol A5 cosmetic blend and mentioned in hair-care product discussions. The hoped-for payoff is a healthier scalp and fuller-looking hair.

Published work on the extract covers memory in rodents and in-vitro antioxidant and antimicrobial tests. No study of hair or scalp appearance was found.
quick.how: It is used as an ingredient in leave-on or rinse-off scalp and hair products, as part of a regular routine.
quick.risks: No hair-specific safety data were found in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Ceylon cinnamon bark extract appears in the cosmetic blend Sepicontrol A5 and in hair-care product discussions, with the idea of supporting the scalp and follicles for fuller-looking hair. Hair or scalp studies were not found.

hydroxypropyl-ammonium-gluconate.summary: A gluconate humectant paired with a gluconamide in bond-building hair products for stronger, smoother-looking hair.

quick.overview:
3-Hydroxypropyl ammonium gluconate is a gluconate salt used with a gluconamide in hair care mixtures promoted for strengthening hair fibres and reducing breakage, for stronger, smoother-looking hair. It also acts as a humectant.

The only published work found is a 2022 crystallography paper that examined how the gluconamide and gluconate interact with amino acids, and stated the mechanism of the mixture on hair was unknown.
quick.how: It is used in bond-building hair treatments and conditioners, typically applied on a regular schedule.
quick.risks: No hair-specific safety data were found in the sources reviewed. Gluconates are salts of gluconic acid, which occurs in fruit, honey and wine.

angle.text: This gluconate salt is paired with a gluconamide in bond-building hair products, promoted for reinforcing hair fibres to cut breakage and leave hair stronger and smoother-looking. The only research found is crystal chemistry.

hydrolyzed-silk-protein.summary: Broken-down silk protein added to conditioners so hair feels softer and looks glossier.

quick.overview:
Hydrolyzed silk protein is silk split into smaller peptides and amino acids, found in conditioners and cleansers. People use it for softer, smoother, shinier-looking hair.

Silk is mostly fibroin with a coating of sericin, and the small fragments are meant to coat the strands. It appears in patents for washing gels and permanent-wave compositions; no human study of hair appearance was found.
quick.how: It is used as an ingredient in conditioners, masks and cleansers, with the effect noticeable after each wash.
quick.risks: No hair-specific safety data were found in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Hydrolyzed silk protein is added to conditioners so small silk peptides coat the strands, leaving hair softer, smoother and glossier after use. Hair trials of the ingredient were not found.

hydrolyzed-keratin.summary: Broken-down keratin added to conditioners and masks to smooth and strengthen damaged hair for a healthier look.

quick.overview:
Hydrolyzed keratin is keratin, from sources such as feathers or wool, cut into small fragments so it dissolves in water. It is added to conditioners and masks to strengthen and smooth damaged hair for a healthier, shinier look.

Proponents say the small protein fragments deposit on or fill gaps in damaged hair. A 120-person trial of a keratin peptide powder for hair health is registered as completed with no results posted; most other published work is on non-cosmetic biomaterials.
quick.how: It is used in conditioners, masks and repair treatments, with the smoothing effect felt after application and often maintained through regular use.
quick.risks: No hair-specific safety findings are described in the sources reviewed. It is an ordinary cosmetic ingredient, and products vary.

angle.text: Hydrolyzed keratin is added to conditioners and repair products so small keratin fragments smooth and strengthen damaged hair for a healthier, shinier look. A registered trial of a keratin peptide powder has no posted results.
